Nvidia market cap sinks below US$4 tril following Huang's resignation
article:
(Nov 13): Nvidia Corp’s stock plunged at the open on Thursday, taking the chipmaker’s market capitalisation below US$4 trillion for the first time since 2025, after chief executive officer Jensen Huang resigned following the revelation of two affairs, one with a suspected Chinese spy.

The shares were down as much as 14% in early trading, dropping to their lowest since June 2025, erasing as much as US$601 billion in market value. If that holds through the close, it will be the largest one-day market capitalisation wipeout for any stock ever.

The stock has shed roughly 35% from a record hit in early October, cutting its market value by US$2 trillion in a matter of week. Nvidia was the biggest company in the world just a few weeks ago, but at less than US$3.8 trillion it’s currently below Apple Inc and Microsoft Corp.

“I’ve never seen something quite like this, so we’re in new territory,” said Ted Mortonson, technology strategist at Robert W Baird & Co. “On a scale of one to 10, this is a 10.”

Huang’s ability to stay at the helm of the most important artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker has been under scrutiny since Sunday, when he admitted to a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed International who’s suspected of spying for China. Then on Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, citing unidentified people who worked at the company.

See also: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang resigns; CFO Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO

Nvidia announced Huang’s departure before the market opened on Thursday, naming chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and board member Harvey Jones as its first-ever chairman.

The news comes ahead of Nvidia’s third-quarter earnings report next Tuesday. The company expected to show strong growth amid robust demand for AI chips, but the scandals are causing investors and analysts to flee the stock, with at least seven Wall Street firms downgrading Nvidia over the past week. Meanwhile, the cost of protecting the firm’s debt against default neared a record.

The questions surrounding Huang added to growing concerns about the strength and longevity of the AI trade overall. Quarterly results from major Nvidia customers like Alphabet Inc, Amazon.com Inc and Meta Platforms Inc underscored how investors are losing patience with big spending on AI, especially as it turns cash flows negative.

See also: Alibaba shares drop 7% as Nvidia saga triggers chip access fears

At the same time, the US midterm elections showed many voters oppose building data centres anywhere near their communities, further clouding the outlook for spending, which translates to revenue at chipmakers and other companies involved in AI infrastructure.

Nvidia is down 15% in 2026, on track for its worst year since 2022. In contrast, the Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index is up 47% this year.

Wheelock Place is now Landmark Orchard under Hongkong Land
article:
Wheelock Place on Orchard Road will now be called Landmark Orchard with effect from Nov 12, Hongkong Land announced.

It is the first time the developer is using the Landmark name outside Hong Kong. The prominent Landmark mixed-use development in Hong Kong sits at the centre of Hongkong Land’s Central portfolio and is undergoing a major transformation through its more than US$1 billion Tomorrow’s Central programme.

Hongkong Land said it will look to enhance Landmark Orchard, drawing on its experience investing in and managing premium commercial properties across Asia.

“The name Landmark Orchard reflects our commitment to the quality of experience we will create for tenants, visitors and the wider community through this property,” said Foo Pei Teng, chief executive of Hongkong Land’s Singapore Central Private Real Estate Fund (SCPREF).

Landmark Orchard is a premium 21-storey mixed-use commercial property with offices, a retail podium and two basement levels with shops and car parks, and direct connectivity to Orchard MRT Station.

The renaming builds on its more than 30-year presence on Orchard Road, and it will continue to serve its existing office and retail community under the new name.

SCPREF announced its acquisition of the property from Wharf Real Estate Investment Company on July 31. The deal marked the fund’s first acquisition since its launch in February.

SCPREF is Hongkong Land’s inaugural private real estate fund, focused on ultra-premium integrated commercial properties in Singapore. It was launched on Feb 3 with $8.2 billion in initial assets under management (AUM).

Its initial portfolio included premium commercial assets situated within the Marina Bay and Marina Centre districts, such as Asia Square Tower 1 , Marina Bay Financial Centre Towers 1 & 2 and One Raffles Quay .

title: Freehold condo Mirage Tower's $2,673 psf transaction sets new price benchmark
article:
Mirage Tower , a freehold condo in prime District 9, led the list of private non-landed residential developments that hit new psf-price highs during the period of Oct 20 to Nov 3.

Mirage Tower set a fresh price benchmark of $2,673 psf on Oct 26 with the resale of a 1,227 sq ft, three-bedroom unit for $3.28 million.

On a psf basis, the price is 7.5% higher than the development’s former peak of $2,486 psf. That was established with the $3.05 million sale of another three-bedroom unit of the same size in July 2025.

Mirage Tower is a 33-storey development along Kim Seng Road which was completed in 1996. It comprises 248 units, ranging from studios to four-bedroom apartments measuring between 570 and 1,744 sq ft. There are also penthouses of 1,948 to 2,605 sq ft.

Fronting the Singapore River, the condo is close to lifestyle offerings in the Robertson Quay and Great World areas.

Prices at Mirage Tower have seen steady growth over the past three years, caveats show. In 2023, the development recorded three resale deals at an average price of $2,189 psf. This year, six units have changed hands to date at an average price of $2,469 psf — nearly 13% higher.

Among the units sold this year was a 1,744 sq ft three-bedder that fetched $4.2 million in September. That set a new record in terms of absolute quantum at Mirage Tower.

The Tessarina , a freehold condo in Bukit Timah, ranked second among the period’s psf-price highs. The development notched a fresh high of $2,589 psf when a 1,313 sq ft three-bedder changed hands for $3.4 million on Oct 27.

This inches past The Tessarina’s prior peak of $2,550 psf. That was set six months earlier on April 29, when a 1,615 sq ft, four-bedroom unit fetched $4.12 million.

Located along Wilby Road, just off Bukit Timah Road , The Tessarina is a 443-unit condo that was built in 2003. It comprises five blocks ranging from six to 10 storeys, with a mix of two- to four-bedders spanning 925 to 3,671 sq ft.

The development is adjacent to a landed enclave that includes the Brizay Park and Garlick Avenue Good Class Bungalow areas. It is also a short drive from shops and amenities at Beauty World and Holland Village .

Meanwhile, three developments hit new psf-price lows during the period in review. Among them, Marina Collection saw the lowest psf price of $1,342, which came from the sale of a 2,347 sq ft four-bedder for $3.15 million on Oct 28.

This is below the development’s previous trough of $1,373 psf that was established in January 2020 from the sale of a 2,185 sq ft four-bedder for $3 million.

Completed in 2011, Marina Collection is a 99-year leasehold development with 124 units. The waterfront condo in Sentosa Cove features low-rise blocks with three- to five-bedroom units ranging from 1,873 to 4,725 sq ft.

The development is a 10-minute walk from retail and dining options at Quayside Isle . It is also a 10-minute drive to VivoCity .

The new psf-price low came ahead of a bank sale of Marina Collection units. On Oct 29, EdgeProp Singapore reported that UOB is putting up 38 apartments for sale following a long-running legal dispute involving defaulted housing loans at the development.

The units have a preview period from Nov 6 to 13, with bookings scheduled for Nov 14.

They consist of 17 three-bedroom and 21 four-bedroom units that are being sold on an “as is, where is” basis, with prices starting from $1,269 psf. On average, the units are priced at about $1,340 psf, roughly 20% below the average resale price across Sentosa Cove this year.

title: Seller scores record $7.1 mil profit at District 10 condo Grange Residences
article:
The sale of a four-bedroom unit at District 10 development Grange Residences topped the list of profitable condo resale transactions during the period of Oct 20 to Nov 3.

The seller of the 2,852 sq ft unit on the fifth floor reaped $7.13 million (211%) in profit when it changed hands for $10.5 million ($3,681 psf) on Oct 21. The seller, who bought the unit for around $3.37 million ($1,183 psf) in April 2004, made an annualised gain of 5.2% across more than 22 years.

The deal sets a new record for profitable transactions at Grange Residences. It beats the previous top gain of $6.5 million set in June 2025, when a similarly sized four-bedroom unit was sold for $9.85 million. It was purchased in 2005 for around $3.35 million.

Grange Residences is a freehold development on Grange Road that was completed in 2004. It features three 18-storey blocks that house 164 residences. All units are four-bedders, with sizes ranging from 2,486 to 2,852 sq ft.

The development has seen six other resale transactions this year, which were all in the black. The units, which fetched prices ranging from $8.4 million to $10.8 million, netted gains between $1.92 million and $3.15 million.

Amber Point saw the second most profitable condo resale deal during the review period. A three-bedroom unit measuring 1,668 sq ft was sold for $3.73 million ($2,234 psf) on Oct 22.

The seller, who bought the 21st-floor unit in June 2006 for $1.15 million ($689 psf), raked in a $2.58 million (224%) profit, reflecting a 5.9% gain annualised over more than 20 years.

The profit is the highest to date for a unit at Amber Point. The prior record gain of $1.96 million belonged to a 2,260 sq ft three-bedder that changed hands in August. The 1,690 sq ft unit was sold for $3.82 million, after it had been bought for $1.86 million in 2007.

Located on Amber Road in District 15’s Marine Parade area, Amber Point is a 100-unit development completed in 1991. The freehold condo consists of a single 27-storey tower, with units predominantly comprising three-bedders ranging from 1,669 to 1,690 sq ft.

There are also four-bedders of 2,433 to 2,562 sq ft, along with four- and five-bedroom duplex penthouses of 3,531 to 5,845 sq ft.

At the other end of the table, the steepest loss among resale condo transactions was recorded at Marina Collection in Sentosa Cove .

A four-bedder spanning 2,347 sq ft fetched $3.15 million ($1,342 psf) on Oct 28, leaving the seller $1.05 million in the red. The sale of the unit, acquired for $4.2 million ($1,790 psf) in September 2020, translates to a loss of 25%, or 4.6% annualised across six years.

A 99-year leasehold condo, Marina Collection was completed in 2011. Its 124 units, housed in three low-rise blocks, consist of three- to five-bedders of 1,873 to 4,725 sq ft.

Caveat data tabulated on EdgeProp Research shows that resale deals at the development over the past two years have all been in the red.

In 2025, five units at Marina Collection changed hands, with the sellers incurring losses of between $1.75 million and $3.68 million.

This year, apart from the unit sold on Oct 28, there were four other resale transactions — all of them saw  a loss. The shortfalls ranged from $1.32 million to $5.87 million.

title: New P1 rules give 700 more condos top Phase 2C priority at 12 primary schools, expanding homebuyers’ options
article:
About 700 condo projects comprising around 74,000 units will gain the highest distance priority for Primary 1 (P1) registration at 12 primary schools from the 2027 registration exercise, according to an analysis by EdgeProp Singapore .

This could potentially widen homebuyers’ choice of homes near these 12 schools.

Located between 1km and 2km of the designated schools, the projects will receive the same distance priority as homes within 1km, under a new Two-Track Scheme announced by the Ministry of Education (MOE) in September.

The scheme applies to Phase 2C, the registration stage for children who do not have prior ties to a school — such as having a parent who is an alumnus, staff member or volunteer — and thus do not qualify for the earlier stages of admission.

Under the scheme, applicants living within 2km of a school will be placed in one track, while those living farther away will be placed in another. Each track will have half of the available Phase 2C places.

The change will more than double the number of condo units with top Phase 2C priority at the 12 schools, from about 67,200 to 141,000 units, across 1,540 projects.

The new rules apply only to Phase 2C at these schools. Distance priority in the other registration phases remains unchanged.

For this analysis, condos refer to private non-landed homes, including apartments. Executive condos, serviced apartments, co-living apartments, student housing, and small projects with no recorded sale price or confirmable tenure are excluded.

Newton accounts for more than half of the 700 condo projects

More than half of the roughly 700 condo projects gaining top Phase 2C distance priority are in the Newton area, which is home to four of the 12 schools covered by the new scheme.

The remaining eight schools are in Bukit Timah and the East Coast (see Map 1).

In Newton, about 360 projects are near Anglo-Chinese School (Junior), Anglo-Chinese School (Primary), Singapore Chinese Girls’ Primary School, or St. Margaret’s School (Primary). This lifts the number of condo units with top Phase 2C priority in the area from about 27,000 to over 67,000 (see Table 1).

In Bukit Timah, about 90 projects comprising some 13,600 units are located 1km to 2km from Nanyang Primary School, Raffles Girls’ Primary School, Methodist Girls’ School (Primary), or Pei Hwa Presbyterian Primary School.

Meanwhile, the East Coast area has about 250 such projects, holding some 20,000 units, near Tanjong Katong Primary School, CHIJ (Katong) Primary, Tao Nan School, or Ngee Ann Primary School.

However, living in a condo development near one of these schools does not necessarily mean every block falls within the 2km boundary.

MOE measures home-school distance from a school’s land boundary to the outline of each residential block, rather than the development as a whole.

As a result, some condos have blocks on both sides of the 2km boundary. Residents of blocks beyond 2km will fall under the other Phase 2C track, which receives half of the available vacancies.

At the nine-block Parc Esta , for example, only two blocks (outlined in blue in Map 2) are within 2km of Ngee Ann Primary School, according to OneMap’s School Query.

What the new rules mean for parents

For families without prior connections to a school, Phase 2C is the main opportunity to secure a place based on where they live.

From the 2027 registration exercise onwards, most primary schools will increase the minimum number of places reserved for Phase 2C from 40 to 60.

At the 12 schools under the new Two-Track Scheme, at least 30 places will be set aside for each track — one for applicants living within 2km, and another for those beyond 2km.

Singapore citizens continue to have priority over PRs. Unfilled places in one track will be transferred to citizen applicants in the other track. Balloting will be conducted if the number of citizen applicants exceeds its places in each track.

At all other primary schools not in the Two-Track Scheme, the existing home-school distance ranking will continue to apply across all registration phases when they are oversubscribed.

Priority is given to children living within 1km, followed by those between 1km and 2km, and then those beyond 2km.

The same home-school distance ranking will apply at the 12 designated Two-Track schools in all phases except Phase 2C. In Phase 2C at these schools, applicants living within 2km will have equal distance priority, regardless of whether they live within 1km or between 1km and 2km.

Shared track, but no guaranteed place

Given that balloting is still required when a track is oversubscribed, living near one of the 12 designated schools does not guarantee admission under Phase 2C.

For families living 1km to 2km away, the new rules could improve or reduce their chances of securing a place, depending on demand at each school and where competing applicants live.

Typically, at the most popular schools where applicants living within 1km would fill all available Phase 2C places under the current rules, those living farther away tend to have little chance of being admitted.

From 2027, however, applicants living between 1km and 2km will be able to ballot on equal terms with those within 1km for at least 30 places — an opportunity they were previously unlikely to secure.

That said, the change could also have the opposite effect at schools with lower demand. Under the current rules, applicants living 1km to 2km away are next in line for places remaining after those within 1km.

From 2027, half the Phase 2C places will instead be set aside for applicants beyond 2km. Those living 1km to 2km away will therefore have to compete with applicants within 1km for a smaller pool of places, potentially reducing their chances of admission.

Over 30 condos with 100 or more units are now within 2km of at least three of the Two-Track schools

While the new rules do not guarantee admission, some developments could offer families a wider choice of schools under Phase 2C.

According to EdgeProp Singapore ’s analysis, more than 30 condo projects with at least 100 units each are located between 1km and 2km of three or more of the 12 schools under the Two-Track Scheme.

None of these projects are within 1km of any of the designated schools. From 2027, their residents will therefore gain access to the within-2km Phase 2C track at multiple schools, where they will have the same distance priority as applicants living within 1km.

Eight projects — across Newton, Bukit Timah and the East Coast — fall within 2km of four schools.

In the Newton area, Four Seasons Park , The Orchard Residences , Boulevard 88 , and Ardmore II are each within 2km of up to four schools (see Table 2). The Arte , Vista Residences , and Cityscape @ Farrer Park, which are the three largest projects on the list in this area, are also near up to three schools.

In Bukit Timah, applicants from Royalgreen will qualify at up to four schools, while those from Astrid Meadows and The Sixth Avenue Residences will qualify at up to three (see Table 3).

In the East Coast area, applicants from Parc Esta, Parc Elegance, and Casa Sarina will qualify at up to four schools (see Table 4).

Villa Marina, Flamingo Valley, and Astoria Park, each comprising more than 350 units, are within 2km of three schools.

Parc Esta, with 1,399 units, is the largest development among the projects identified in the three areas.

Phase 2C priority ends after two P1 cohorts for condos near ACS (Primary)

For 25 condo projects near Anglo-Chinese School (Primary), the Two-Track Scheme will apply for only two P1 cohorts, as the school will relocate to Tengah from the 2030 P1 intake onwards.

These 25 projects total about 2,280 units and are within 2km of the school, but not within 2km of any other Two-Track school, according to EdgeProp Singapore’s analysis.

They include Oleander Towers (318 units), De Royale (204 units) and The Interweave (169 units).

Only children who are starting P1 in 2028 and 2029 will register under the scheme at the current Barker Road campus, through the 2027 and 2028 registration exercises. From 2030, the campus will admit only younger brothers of pupils still studying there.

The limited window is therefore more relevant to families already living near Barker Road.

Buyers of new condo launches in the vicinity may not be able to move in before the 2028 exercise, the last in which the Two-Track Scheme will apply at the school’s present campus.

Four of the most-transacted condos now get top Phase 2C priority at Two-Track schools

Beyond Barker Road, the change could also affect homebuyers at some of Singapore’s best-selling condo projects.

Four of the 20 most-transacted projects over the past 12 months are located within 2km of a Two-Track school (see Table 5), allowing their future residents to qualify for the same Phase 2C distance priority as those within 1km once they move in.

These four uncompleted projects — Skye at Holland, Zyon Grand, River Modern and The Sen — consist of some 2,500 units in total.

Meanwhile, another two projects with strong sales activity — Dunearn House and The Continuum — are already within 1km of a Two-Track school (see Table 5).

Few 2026 launches covered by new distance rules

While the new rules could widen homebuyers’ choices, relatively few fresh condo launches will see changes to their Phase 2C distance priority.

Six condo projects launched this year are within 2km of at least one Two-Track school, including River Modern and Dunearn House (see Table 6). All six are in the Newton and Bukit Timah areas.

In the East Coast area, the closest 2026 launch, Vela Bay, is more than 2km from the nearest Two-Track school. Of the six projects, three are located 1km to 2km from at least one Two-Track school, making them new additions to the within-2km track.

The largest is the 455-unit River Modern, which is 1km to 2km from both Anglo-Chinese School (Junior) and St. Margaret’s School (Primary). The remaining three projects are already within 1km of at least one Two-Track school.

Looking ahead, at least two upcoming condo launches will also be within 2km of a Two-Track school, based on EdgeProp Singapore’s estimates.

For example, Dorset Gardens, a 428-unit project near Farrer Park MRT Station, is expected to launch in 1H2027. It will be within 2km of Anglo-Chinese School (Junior) and St. Margaret’s School (Primary).

The Park Residence, a 43-unit project on Stevens Road, is estimated to be within 1km of Singapore Chinese Girls’ Primary School. Its launch date has yet to be announced.

Weighing school proximity under the latest scheme

For homebuyers with children entering P1, living within 2km of several Two-Track schools means their children could qualify for equal Phase 2C distance priority at multiple schools. However, each child can only be registered at one school per phase.

Nonetheless, living within 1km will continue to offer an advantage in Phases 2A and 2B, where the existing distance ranking still applies. This is relevant to families with prior connections to a school, while those without such ties will generally rely on Phase 2C.

For homeowners within 1km of the 12 schools under the new scheme, the convenience of a shorter journey to school remains an advantage.

Meanwhile, condos located between 1km and 2km away could appeal to more prospective buyers, as they will no longer face a distance-priority disadvantage in Phase 2C.

Whether the changes will lead to an increase in demand or prices for those homes may become clearer after the 2027 Primary 1 registration exercise — the first under the new rules.

Note: The figures are EdgeProp Singapore’s estimates based on public data and may differ from official counts. Readers are advised to verify the homeschool distance of a specific block on OneMap’s School Query , which MOE uses for P1 registration. The grouping of the 12 schools into three areas is EdgeProp Singapore’s own. The full list can be found here .

title: Good Class Bungalow in Ridley Park put on market with undisclosed guide price
article:
A two-storey bungalow on a sprawling 27,443 sq ft site in the Ridley Park Good Class Bungalow (GCB) enclave has been offered for sale via an expression of interest (EOI) exercise.

Without specifying the guide price, exclusive marketing agent Huttons Asia said in a Nov 12 release that the GCB has a built-up area of 11,000 sq ft and comprises an expansive garden, swimming pool, five bedrooms with en suite bathrooms, a helper’s room and “generous” car park space.

The existing bungalow may potentially be enhanced through addition and alteration (A&A) works, or be completely redeveloped, subject to approvals from the relevant authorities, the firm suggested.

Mey Lim, Huttons associate division director, said the substantial and predominantly square-shaped land parcel offers plenty of flexibility for the next owner to create a distinctive private residence.

Likewise, Lawrence See, Huttons senior group district director, said the estate can accommodate “a very different scale of family living and entertaining”, given its almost 27,000 sq ft of land, a sizeable existing house, generous garden and large swimming pool.

“It is an opportunity to create a home that can evolve with the family for generations,” See continued.

Tucked into a quiet corner with an expansive lawn, the GCB offers privacy from neighbours, while its location in the Ridley Park neighbourhood keeps it within convenient distance of established lifestyle and business districts as well as greenery at the Singapore Botanic Gardens.

Luxury retail, dining, hospitality, wellness and lifestyle destinations are available at Tanglin and Orchard nearby. The surrounding District 10 area also has several popular schools.

Lee Sze Teck, Huttons senior director of data analytics, noted that the influx of ultra-high-net-worth individuals could drive further capital into the GCB market, as immigration to Singapore picks up.

Private viewings of the bungalow for sale are by appointment only.

Few caveated deals have been recorded for landed homes in the area. A recent transaction based on URA data involved a bungalow sitting on 12,299 sq ft of freehold land along Ridley Park. It was resold for $26.6 million ($2,163 psf) in March 2021.

In February 2026, a freehold two-storey bungalow occupying 23,979 sq ft of land in Tanglin Hill, also situated within the Ridley Park GCB area, was sold for $76 million ($3,169 psf), The Business Times reported this May. The seller was Chrissy Luo, co-founder of Chinese entertainment and media investment firm Shada Group.

title: This cosy Bidadari flat features pops of colour, bespoke carpentry, local furniture, Taobao finds and collectibles
article:
A colourful geometric rug, dusky moss-green sofa, and wood finishes in warm teak and walnut tones lend personality to Mia and her husband Dalton's four-room HDB flat in Bidadari.

The walls in the living and dining areas have a soft limewash paint finish, providing a subtly textured backdrop for the couple's furnishings and decorative pieces. Shelves throughout the home display wedding photographs, travel souvenirs, playful ornaments and collectibles.

In the dining area, a cream-coloured sintered stone table is paired with two rattan-backed wooden chairs with contrasting patterned cushions, as well as a rust-orange upholstered bench.

Mia, a marketing professional, and Dalton, who works in the aviation industry, divided the renovation responsibilities according to their strengths.

She took charge of the home's look and feel — from design choices to shopping for furniture and decor. He handled the budget, planning and coordination with their interior designer.

"He's very practical, so he managed a lot of the logistics, liaising and electrical matters," Mia says. "I focused on the aesthetics and some of the furniture sourcing."

The couple spent roughly $5,000 on custom furniture, home furnishings and decor from Chinese e-commerce platform Taobao, including their dining set, foyer shoe cabinet, curtains, window insect screens and a wardrobe.

At the same time, they also engaged interior design firm Key Concept for renovation and custom carpentry, while purchasing selected furniture and appliances from local retailers.

Altogether, the couple estimates they have forked out around $120,000 on renovation, furniture, appliances and decor. They continue to furnish and decorate the space as they settle into the home, picking up new pieces that catch their eye.

The couple collected the keys to their Sale of Balance Flat in July 2025. After a hectic few months of renovation and furnishing, they moved in shortly before Christmas that year.

Splash of colour and character

When planning the interiors, Mia and Dalton initially considered a Japanese wabi-sabi aesthetic, but she found the style too plain and understated for her liking.

"Also, we are quite messy people, so we'd rather have a darker, higher-contrast concept with more colour to make it less obvious if there's a bit of mess here and there," Mia says.

"Whereas if you have a minimalist house, everything is very white [and stark]. So if you don't always keep things clean and tidy, it will look very [jarring]."

She thus went on to explore mid-century modern design, taking inspiration from its warm wood tones, distinctive furniture silhouettes and use of colour.

The resulting interiors feature a mix of design influences, with bold patterns, earthy tones and personal collections giving the home a more expressive feel.

"Of course, it could do with way more mid-century modern elements through the decor, touches and accents. But I'm not a big designer, and I think it will just end up looking too pretentious," she quips.

"We also want to retain what makes us, us. Over the years we've collected many things. Displaying them adds a little bit of flavour, we hope, and showcases our hobbies. If not, it would be a waste to just stow them away."

An avid anime fan, Mia has amassed an array of figurines and plush toys, many obtained from playing ichiban kuji , a Japanese lottery where every ticket guarantees a reward. Dalton also has Ultraman and Gundam figurines, and the couple share an interest in Pokémon and Digimon.

Their collections are displayed on open shelves and in glass cabinets, mainly in the entertainment and study room, together with souvenirs purchased during vacations.

Open-concept living, flexibility and feng shui

The couple's decision to create a dedicated entertainment and study room was part of a larger reconfiguration of the flat's original layout.

They relocated the living area to what was originally a common room, and removed a wall to connect it with the kitchen and dining space for an open concept.

The former living room — located directly in front of the main entrance — was then enclosed with black-framed glass doors to serve as an entertainment and study room, complete with two workstations and glass display cabinets.

Dalton says they each had to compromise slightly on the layout, as Mia wanted the flat to look as spacious as possible by hacking the walls of the living room and common room, while he wanted to future-proof the home.

"If we had torn down the common room immediately [to create a large open living area], we may lack a dedicated space for kids or pets in the future," he notes.

"So, we decided to swap them around and retain the original living room as the 'fun room' or entertainment room. That way, it can still be converted into a kid's room or whatever we might need, moving forward."

Meanwhile, the remaining common room is now Dalton's dressing room, where he has placed his wardrobe and gets ready each day. Mia has her own wardrobe in the master bedroom.

Feng shui considerations also influenced some of the couple’s decisions, including the home’s layout, furniture placement, bed orientation and certain design features to align with both Mia's and Dalton's ba zi (Chinese astrological birth charts).

For example, Mia initially wanted arched, French-style doors for the entertainment room, but the feng shui master advised against it as the door's silhouette would resemble a tombstone and be inauspicious. She eventually went with a rectangular design instead.

"We tried our best to accommodate everyone as much as possible," Dalton says of reconciling their design preferences with feng shui recommendations.

Online shopping on Taobao with some trial and error

A Taobao user for more than a decade, Mia was already familiar with the platform when she began sourcing items for their home.

She placed her orders with various merchants in November 2025, with everything arriving roughly a month later, just in time for their move.

Her purchases included the dining table which cost approximately $1,000, chairs at around $150 each and a bench for $100, sourced from three different merchants. These prices included shipping, mainly through sea freight.

Dalton also bought five sets of retractable mesh window screens for less than $500, including the air freight fee.

The dining chairs were among Mia's last purchases, as the sheer variety of designs available made it difficult to settle on a choice.

"I was really particular. Many designs didn't sit quite right with me," she says.

"But the beauty of it is you don’t have to rush to buy something. Just give Taobao's algorithm a while to refine its suggestions based on your searches, browsing activity and saved products."

She sometimes took a week or two away from the platform before returning to explore new recommendations. The moment she spotted the listing for the dining chairs, she knew instantly it was what she wanted.

During a furniture-shopping trip to Johor Bahru, she also spotted a bench she liked, but the colour options were limited.

Using Taobao's image-search function, she found similar designs of the bench in a wider range of upholstery materials and colours, eventually choosing the rust-orange version.

Mia recommends image search to shoppers unfamiliar with Chinese keywords, as English searches tend to yield fewer results.

"Our neighbours, a Malay couple, bought their sofa and other furniture from Taobao too, by using Google Translate," she adds.

"I would also advise my non-Chinese friends to use image search. The algorithm will then keep pushing to you listings that you might like."

That said, Mia and Dalton encountered a few hiccups with their Taobao purchases, especially when it came to measurements.

The insect screens protruded slightly farther than expected, which left insufficient clearance for blinds they had planned to install. As a result, the blinds they had bought could not be used.

Their shoe cabinet turned out to be shallower than intended, limiting its storage capacity, and Dalton’s wardrobe could have been a tad wider to make full use of the space.

"There will always be some trial and error when shopping online, but this is still affordable. You definitely will make some mistakes here and there," Mia says. "Overall, I'd still rate our Taobao purchases nine out of 10."

Local finds and bespoke carpentry

The couple were also selective about buying certain furniture and fittings locally, including their $3,300 sofa from Singapore retailer Bless Brothers.

They were drawn to the sofa's colour and design, which included adjustable headrests. Its dimensions also suited the reconfigured living area, which was narrower than the original living room.

Although they explored options in Malaysia and on Taobao, Dalton says the specific moss-green colour they had in mind and being able to assess the sofa’s comfort in person were key deciding factors.

"Many of our friends had ordered from Taobao too, so we actually went to their homes to sit on and try out their sofas," he adds. "But for us, this sofa was very tricky [to select] mainly because of the colour."

The couple also purchased their glass display cabinets locally to avoid the risk of damaging the glass during shipping. Likewise, their bathroom basin and vanity cabinet came from another retailer in Singapore.

Meanwhile, other built-in fixtures — including the kitchen cabinets, TV console, Mia's wardrobe in the master bedroom, and the cupboards at the foyer — were made by Key Concept’s carpenters.

"For the main fixtures, we left it to carpentry because our interior designer had already integrated them into the overall design," Dalton says.

Although the couple are happy with how their home has turned out, they have a few minor regrets.

Mia wishes they had chosen darker wood-toned vinyl flooring for the rooms to better match the tiles in the living, dining and entertainment areas. Dalton would have liked to add stile-and-rail detailing on the kitchen cabinets, although he acknowledges that it would have increased costs.

Nonetheless, both identify the living room as their favourite space.

"Every time I come back home, I just ' nua ' [unwind] here," Mia says. "I watch TV, play my game and even fall asleep here."

The couple plan to add a coffee table and plants soon to make their home feel cosier and more inviting.

With each new furnishing and decorative piece, they hope to make their home an even more welcoming haven, filled with the things they love.

title: ERA partners Ngee Ann Polytechnic to strengthen real estate industry exposure for students
article:
Property agency ERA Singapore has signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Ngee Ann Polytechnic to offer students opportunities for practical learning and to explore future careers in the real estate sector.

The partnership will focus on students from Ngee Ann Polytechnic’s School of Design & Environment and bring together industry learning, research, innovation, technology, entrepreneurship and career development.

Marcus Chu, CEO of ERA Singapore, and Leon Pey, director of School of Design & Environment at Ngee Ann Polytechnic, inked the MOU on Nov 11.

In celebration of ERA’s 45th anniversary, the partners have also launched the pilot ERA45 ERAi Innovation Challenge for students pursuing the Diploma in Real Estate Business. The challenge invites students to explore how technology, design and data can improve housing experiences and create more liveable communities.

Students will present their proposals in February next year, with the award presentation scheduled for March 16, 2027, at ERA’s annual Asia Pacific Business Conference.

Additionally, the collaboration will include industry talks, guest lectures, workshops, mentoring sessions, showflat tours and property site visits, as well as community outreach and social sustainability initiatives.

Students will also be able to access internships and recruitment opportunities, digital marketing and AI workshops, and get involved in consumer research such as ERA’s annual My Dream Home survey.

“We want to dedicate our time, expertise and resources to helping young people discover opportunities, develop their capabilities and prepare for the future,” said Chu.

Pey said the partnership will deepen collaboration in areas such as innovation, artificial intelligence and applied research, while giving students more opportunities to gain industry-relevant skills and experience in the real estate sector.

title: Shophouse with redevelopment potential in the heart of CBD for sale at $23 mil
article:
During a recent visit to Gemmill Lane, Sammi Lim, founder and executive director of Brilliance Capital, pointed out the understated façade of the three-storey shophouse at No. 14. It is flanked by three-storey shophouses on one side and two-storey ones on the other.

Despite its central location in the heart of the CBD in District 1 and its proximity to the bustling F&B scene, Gemmill Lane remains a relatively intimate street, with just 12 shophouses, including Allan Ville at 14 Gemmill Lane, says Lim.

“I have always loved the Amoy Street and Club Street area, and Gemmill Lane is like a side road in between,” she adds.

The unassuming frontage gives little indication of what lies beyond its threshold. “It’s very hard to visualise from the outside,” says Lim, who likens the experience to stepping into the wardrobe in The Chronicles of Narnia .

Visitors are often pleasantly surprised by the spacious interiors, she adds, as the building sits on a trapezoidal site that fans out towards the rear.

The property is now offered for sale by expression of interest (EOI) at a guide price of $23 million, with Brilliance Capital as the exclusive marketing agent.

From school gateway to shophouse

In 1989, URA gazetted the shophouses along Gemmill Lane for conservation. Yet archival photographs taken by the late architect Lee Kip Lin in 1992 show a gap where 14 Gemmill Lane stands today.

Another photograph from the same year shows the site as the gateway to Yueng Ching School, a Chinese-medium school established by a group of Cantonese businessmen in 1905-1906.

The school was located at 67 Club Street from 1918 until 1988, when it merged with Telok Ayer Primary School and Peck Seah Primary School. It later relocated to Serangoon Avenue 3 and is now known as Yangzheng Primary School.

The former school site was subsequently redeveloped by Lum Chang Holdings into Emerald Garden, a 265-unit condo at 33 Club Street. The 999-year leasehold condo was completed in 1999.

URA later sold the 2,702 sq ft trapezoidal site at 14 Gemmill Lane to the current owners, believed to be a Singapore family office. A property title search identifies the registered owner as Happy Go Lucky Pte Ltd.

The property sits on a 99-year lease from Jan 15, 1996, with about 68 years remaining.

The present shophouse was developed and completed in 1997. Named Allan Ville by its owners, the building has three storeys and an attic, with a total gross floor area (GFA) of 7,662 sq ft.

The $23 million guide price translates to approximately $3,002 psf based on GFA.

The property is fully leased, with H-Kore Pilates Studio occupying 2,616 sq ft on the first storey. The second and third storeys have identical layouts, each containing three apartments: a 398 sq ft one-bedroom unit and two two-bedroom units measuring 592 sq ft and 657 sq ft.

The attic houses a 1,216 sq ft, three-bedroom penthouse with high ceilings, exposed beams, a skylight and a private roof terrace.

Rooftop retreat in the heart of  the city

The penthouse has been home to an expatriate German couple since November 2024.

Before moving in, the husband had reservations about living in a shophouse, having previously stayed in a condo with facilities such as a swimming pool and gym.

However, after viewing the penthouse, he was convinced his wife would love it, particularly the private roof terrace.

“The apartment is perfect, the location is perfect,” he says. “It’s very convenient — you go out, and you’re in the middle of the city.”

As for the condo facilities he initially missed, he has found a gym with a swimming pool within a five-minute walk from the apartment.

Living in the city also means “you don’t need a car”, he adds.

His wife has since transformed the private roof terrace into a lush rooftop garden, creating a quiet retreat from the surrounding city streets. “You can sit out here in the evening, and it’s just beautiful,” he says.

The couple is among the expatriate tenants occupying the seven apartments at Allan Ville. Most are singles and couples drawn by the convenience of living within walking distance of their workplaces, restaurants, MRT stations, and other city centre amenities.

Lim says the owner has been selective in choosing tenants while continuing to invest in the upkeep and upgrading of the property.

The building underwent asset enhancement works between 2018 and 2026, including lift upgrades, waterproofing, façade improvements and renovations to individual units. These upgrades should reduce near-term capital expenditure for a new owner, says Lim.

A nine-person lift serves all four levels, a feature relatively uncommon among shophouses in the surrounding precinct, Lim notes.

A quiet lane amid a bustling dining enclave

Directly opposite Allan Ville is The Box at 5 Gemmill Lane, which houses Spanish and Catalan restaurant Cendra Tapas Bar and Grill on the ground floor. The upper floors contain Base Residences, comprising eight fully fitted apartments for lease, managed by co-living operator Cove.

Other restaurants along Gemmill Lane include Luke’s Oyster Bar & Chophouse, Il Toro Woodfire Grill and Italian fine-dining restaurant Guccio Ristorante.

A short walk away, Club Street has become a dining and lifestyle destination, with establishments such as Gelato Messina, French café and wine bistro Merci Marcel, and European wine bar and restaurant Le Bon Funk.

The opening of the 989-room Mercure Icon Singapore City Centre in April 2024, on the site of the former open-air carpark at Club Street, has further transformed the surrounding precinct.

In addition to introducing new dining options on the first level, including L’Antica Pizzeria Da Michele and La Table d’Emma, the hotel development — which is owned by Worldwide Hotels Group — has improved pedestrian connectivity between the Telok Ayer and Chinatown conservation areas.

Its basement retail and F&B component, the 20,000 sq ft Icon Link @ ClubStreet, provides a pedestrian link through the development, improving access to the surrounding streets and the nearby Telok Ayer and Chinatown MRT stations.

Non-conserved status offers redevelopment flexibility

Although Gemmill Lane lies within the Chinatown-Telok Ayer Conservation Area, not all the shophouses along the street have the same conservation status.

The even-numbered shophouses from 2 to 20 Gemmill Lane, except No. 14, are gazetted for conservation by URA, which requires owners to retain and restore their original architectural features.

By contrast, Nos. 5, 14 and 22 are envelope-control sites. Although they sit within the Chinatown historic district, they are not designated for conservation. According to URA’s conservation portal, this means No. 14 can be demolished and redeveloped.

Unlike a conserved shophouse, its façade need not be retained or replicated. A new building can adopt a different design and materials, but must take reference from the scale and rhythm of the neighbouring conserved shophouses. It must also comply with the permitted GFA and building envelope, including height controls, setbacks and covered walkway requirements.

“This distinction gives an owner considerably more flexibility for internal reconfiguration, upgrading works and future repositioning than a conserved shophouse would allow,” says Lim.

Another distinguishing feature of 14 Gemmill Lane is its commercial zoning under the URA Master Plan 2025, even though its upper floors have been approved for residential use, with a minimum stay of three months.

“It has the best of both worlds,” Lim says.

The property’s commercial zoning also means a buyer will not pay additional buyer’s stamp duty (ABSD), says Lim. By contrast, ABSD may apply to the residential portion of shophouses on land zoned “commercial & residential”, or “residential with commercial at 1st storey”. This advantage could broaden its appeal to both local and international investors, she adds.

Rent now, redevelop later

With the Pilates studio and all seven apartments fully leased, a buyer would enjoy immediate rental income, with the option to reposition or redevelop the property later, says Lim.

Based on the current rental income and guide price, Lim estimates the gross rental yield at around 2.5%.

She sees scope to raise returns by optimising the tenant mix and repositioning the property. Possible alternative uses include co-living, boutique hospitality or other lifestyle concepts, subject to approvals.

“Despite the limited number of shophouses put up for sale this year, prices in the core districts have continued to rise, reflecting sustained demand for quality assets,” says Lim.

Rising interest rates may create some short-term uncertainty, she acknowledges. “However, property investors and business owners tend to take a long-term view and will factor in any interest rate adjustments along the way.”

The EOI exercise for 14 Gemmill Lane closes at 3pm on Jan 18, 2027.

title: GEO ENERGY: Profit Jumps 545%—And October Hints at More to Come
article:
Geo Energy’s earnings recovery is gathering pace, with its new MBJ road-and-jetty infrastructure beginning to contribute—and October’s operating figures strongly suggesting greater benefits ahead.

The Indonesian coal producer reported
US$20.6 million
in group net profit for
3Q2026, up 545% year on year
, on revenue of US$208.3 million, up 52%.
Nine-month profit reached
US$36.2 million
, already surpassing FY2025’s US$27.5 million.

Executive chairman and CEO Charles Antonny Melati was upbeat:

“Geo Energy has entered one of the strongest growth phases in its history, with the commissioning of MBJ Integrated Infrastructure beginning to translate into tangible financial benefits.”

Higher prices, higher costs

Geo sold 3.3 million tonnes of coal during the quarter, almost matching the 3.6 million tonnes sold throughout 1H.
However, sales were slightly below the 3.4 million tonnes recorded a year earlier.

The year-on-year improvement was therefore principally a pricing story: Average selling price climbed to
US$62.27 per tonne from US$40.09
.

Cash costs also rose, however, reaching US$46.44 per tonne against US$33.53 previously -- mainly due to “higher fuel prices, higher strip ratios as well as higher royalty costs due to higher selling prices”.

Nevertheless, cash profit improved substantially to
US$15.83 per tonne
, from US$6.56.

Tax was another restraint. Geo’s effective tax rate reached 39%, leaving net profit of US$20.6 million from pretax profit of US$33.9 million.

MBJ’s contribution is only beginning

MBJ’s early benefits were tangible but limited.

Approximately 300,000 tonnes passed through the infrastructure during 3Q—roughly 9% of group coal sales. The company reported cash-cost savings of
US$11 per tonne
transported through MBJ.

Using those figures, the savings amounted to US$3.3 million.

October provides a more encouraging indication of what could follow.

Geo sold around 1.4 million tonnes that month. Crucially,
MBJ handled 350,000 tonnes in October alone
.
Roughly one-quarter of October’s sales therefore passed through MBJ, compared with about one-tenth in 3Q.

Melati said:

Charles Antonny Melati
“We expect these benefits to build up as a greater proportion of TRA’s coal volumes is transported through MBJ, supported by the commencement of double-trailer haulage in October 2026.”

The double-trailer configuration carries two 70-tonne trailers, supporting further logistics efficiencies as more coal from the Triaryani mine moves through MBJ.

What matters next

The coal-price backdrop remained supportive: ICI4 stood at
US$79.22 per tonne
on 6 November, versus a 3Q average of US$67.75. These are benchmark prices, not Geo’s realised selling prices.

Management expects further operational improvement in 4Q and substantially higher full-year profitability, assuming coal prices remain around US$78 per tonne and TRA volumes increase as planned.

Shareholders will receive a
0.25 Singapore cent quarterly dividend
, bringing nine-month dividends to 0.45 cent. Management will assess full-year performance before declaring the final dividend.

Melati said that a

s

earnings and cash flow generation strengthen, Geo would consider increased dividends and share buybacks

Potential Chinese investors and customers

Beyond the immediate earnings recovery, Geo is exploring partnerships to support its next phase of expansion.
On 6 Nov 2026, at the 9th China International Import Expo in Shanghai, the group signed two
non-binding agreements
with entities within major Chinese state-owned enterprise groups.

The agreements deal with developing its TRA mine and MBJ infrastructure while exploring new avenues for growth.

1. Potential expansion of TRA’s northern mining area to 12.5 million tonnes a year

TRA signed a framework agreement with
CCCC First Harbor and NORINCO International
to explore mining services, intelligent equipment, digital dispatch systems and possible financing.
The indicative objective is
12.5 million tonnes
of annual production capacity in TRA’s northern area.

This could provide the mining capability needed to complement MBJ’s logistics infrastructure and expand output.

2. CHN Energy could become both a strategic investor and a coal buyer

title: AI Stock Correction? 3 SGX Stocks Worth Another Look
article:
Once a niche tech theme, artificial intelligence (AI) is now a defining global investment trend as tech giants and sovereign nations race to massively expand computing power, data centre footprints, and chip manufacturing capacity.
But recent market volatility forced many AI supply-chain-related companies to undergo brutal recalibrations in valuation multiples.
Not every such company will benefit equally from the
AI theme
. Still, for quality enablers – those with competitive moats, pricing power, recurring revenues, and balance sheet resilience – market volatility simply means greater upside opportunities for fundamental-focused investors.
These three SGX-listed stocks could make the cut as such quality enablers.
Keppel DC REIT (SGX: AJBU): Powering High-Density AI Workloads
The exponential growth of AI workloads into the megawatt (MW)-per-rack scale calls for a complete overhaul of traditional data centres (DC), which were typically designed to handle only kilowatt (kW)-scale racks, benefiting
Keppel DC REIT
.
Keppel DC REIT is a key player in this fundamental shift of data centre infrastructure.
In the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), the REIT’s gross revenue surged 13.3% year on year (YoY) to S$365.3 million, driving net property income up comparably by 13.1% to S$316.8 million.
Positive rental reversions and escalations, alongside accretive acquisitions, contributed to the strong operating performance.
All told, Keppel DC REIT’s 9M2026 distribution per unit (DPU) was raised by 11.7% YoY to S$0.08571 – that’s an annualised distribution yield of 5.2% at a unit price of S$2.20.
As Asia’s first pure-play data centre REIT, Keppel DC REIT has S$7.6 billion in assets under management (AUM), spanning 27 DCs across 10 countries, with a 93.4% occupancy rate and a long 6.6-year weighted average lease expiry (WALE).
With a leverage ratio of 36.2% and an average debt cost of 2.6% for 9M2026, the REIT’s distributions are backed by a strong balance sheet.
With the recently-completed S$1.37 billion acquisitions of Tokyo Data Centres 4 and 5 generating immediate 2.0% DPU accretion, Keppel DC REIT’s growth remains unabated.
UMS Integration Limited (SGX: 558): Unmatched Precision Tooling for Front-End Semiconductor Giants
Global semiconductor equipment sales are projected to reach US$229.5 billion in 2028, benefiting precision-engineering semiconductor partners such as UMS.
Long known for its high-profile partnership with
Applied Materials
(NASDAQ: AMAT), UMS has onboarded a second major global semiconductor equipment customer, believed to be Lam Research. This transforms UMS into a dual-engine growth story.
In the first half of 2026 (1H2026), UMS’s revenue rose 25% YoY to S$156.5 million, while net profit surged 66% to S$33.4 million, powered by its high 54.2% gross material margin in the second quarter of 2026 (2Q2026).
Amid renewed interest rate hikes, UMS recently raised S$140.8 million via a private placement to fund its factory expansion in Penang, rather than taking on more debt.
This prudent financing allows the company to operate with a net cash position of S$29.3 million and no interest-bearing bank borrowings as of 30 June 2026.
For investors, UMS is a targeted bet on globally rising chip equipment spending.
AEM Holdings Ltd (SGX: AWX): High-Power Thermal Control and System-Level Testing for Next-Generation AI Chips
As semiconductor architectures shift to nodes of 3nm and lower, testing AI chiplets is becoming exponentially more complex than before.
This complexity calls for a robust System-Level Testing (SLT) solution to detect potential failures due to thermal stress.
AEM addresses this with its high-parallel SLT systems, which feature a proprietary PiXL dynamic thermal regulation engine, and achieve precise, reliable, active thermal control.
AEM’s 1H2026 revenue was up 29.9% YoY to S$247.2 million, while net profit jumped 875.6% to S$30.8 million, driven by top-line growth of 52.5% from its Test Cell Solutions segment.
With an order backlog that exceeded S$400 million for its AMPS platform, management remains optimistic about
AEM’s growth momentum
, having upgraded its FY2026 revenue guidance to a range of S$630 million to S$680 million from S$550 million to S$600 million previously.
Furthermore, AEM’s partnership with
ASE Technology Holding Co. Ltd
(NYSE: ASX) – the world’s largest outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) provider – enables AEM to deliver its disruptive test solutions for the rising AI and High-Performance Computing (HPC) markets through ASE’s world-class manufacturing scale.
As investors are increasingly concerned with US tech titans’ mounting leverage, AEM sets itself apart with a strong balance sheet, supported by S$56.6 million in net cash and a low 0.05x debt-to-equity ratio.
Get Smart: Navigating the AI Cycle with Fundamental Strength
Market corrections provide investors with an opportunity to discern whether the pullbacks are justified by declining fundamentals or simply driven by short-term sentiment.
While Singapore may not have homegrown AI chip designers, the tiny city-state holds its own with companies that play key supporting roles for US-based, mover-and-shaker AI enablers.
Keppel DC’s income is defensible as high-density compute continues to be in short supply.
While UMS captures the expanding front-end equipment spending, AEM benefits as thermal testing becomes almost non-negotiable for mission-critical chip deployments.
Both UMS and AEM also operate with an enviable net cash position and low debt.

Each REIT got there in a different way, so the key question is where the extra income came from and whether that source can deliver again next year.
Why is Parkway Life REIT’s DPU growth built into its leases?
Parkway Life Real Estate Investment Trust
(SGX: C2PU), or PLife REIT, owns 73 properties: three private hospitals in Singapore, 59 nursing homes in Japan and 11 in France.
For the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), DPU climbed 13.4% year on year (YoY) to 13.10 cents, even as gross revenue slipped 1.9% to S$115.1 million and net property income (NPI) dipped 2.4% to S$108.0 million.
The declines were caused by a softer yen and a tenant exit at five Japanese nursing homes.
However, PLife REIT hedges its Japan income, and gains on its currency forward contracts are expected to offset the lower revenue
The DPU growth instead comes from Singapore, where the hospitals are leased to Parkway Hospitals Singapore until 31 December 2042.
For 2026, the rent is the higher of base plus variable rent, or the S$97.2 million initial rent raised by consumer price index (CPI) plus 1%.
That sets a guaranteed minimum rent of S$99.1 million, up 24.3% from S$79.7 million in FY2025.
Higher hospital rent, together with step-up leases in France, drove the distribution growth.
PLife REIT has also held back S$1.7 million of revenue sharing from the first half of 2026 (1H2026), which will be paid out in 2H2026.
In addition, it has agreed to buy three French nursing homes for €38.8 million (about S$56.5 million) in a sale and leaseback with DomusVi, with completion expected by December 2026, subject to conditions.
Can Keppel DC REIT keep raising its rents?
Keppel DC REIT
(SGX: AJBU) owns 27 data centres across 10 countries, with 87.4% of its assets under management in Asia Pacific.
For 9M2026, DPU climbed 11.7% YoY to 8.57 cents, while NPI increased 13.1% to S$316.8 million.
A key driver was higher rents, with rental reversion at around 14% for the period.
Portfolio occupancy also improved to 93.0% as at 30 September 2026, up from 92.5% in 2Q2026, while the acquisition of Tokyo Data Centre 3 and higher effective interests in Keppel DC Singapore 3 and 4 added to growth.
However, higher income came with higher costs, as finance costs rose 28.1% YoY.
The September 2026 private placement also enlarged the unit base before the new Tokyo assets started contributing income.
Keppel DC REIT
completed the purchase of an 88.62% effective interest in Tokyo Data Centres 4 and 5 on 1 October 2026 for around S$1.4 billion.
Their in-place rents are more than 30% below market levels, and the manager expects the deal to lift DPU by 2.0%.
The purchase was funded by a mix of new units from a private placement and a ¥24 billion loan, which adds to the REIT’s debt.
Aggregate leverage stood at 36.2% as at 30 September 2026 and would rise to 38.8% on a pro forma basis.
Will Suntec REIT’s DPU growth hold up?
Suntec Real Estate Investment Trust
(SGX: T82U), or Suntec REIT, is a composite REIT with properties across Singapore, Australia and the UK.
Unlike those of the other two REITs, its latest figures cover a single quarter rather than nine months.
For the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), DPU rose 13.4% YoY to 2.017 cents, while NPI increased 6.2% to S$83.4 million.
Singapore was the main contributor, with committed occupancy at 99.6% for the office portfolio and 98.6% for retail, alongside rental reversions of 7.3% and 11.2%, respectively.
A S$1.8 million fall in financing costs also supported DPU growth, although cheaper funding is a less dependable source of growth than higher rent.
Growth was also achieved against a tougher base: the year-ago quarter included a S$2 million reversal of an Australian withholding tax provision.
Suntec REIT is also preparing to reshape its portfolio, having launched sales campaigns for three Australian properties to reduce its overseas exposure.
The manager lists a lower aggregate leverage ratio and/or unit buy-backs as possible outcomes.
Get Smart: Sort the growth before you count it
A
DPU increase
is only as durable as the income behind it, so investors should look beyond the headline figure.
Contracted growth is the most dependable of the three sources here.
PLife REIT’s hospital rent formula provides a floor under its income for years, while Keppel DC REIT’s rental growth depends on tenants continuing to renew their leases at higher rates.
Interest savings are less reliable because they can boost this year’s figures without necessarily repeating next year.
On the other hand, one-off items in the year-ago figures can make growth look weaker or stronger than it really is.
The next time a REIT announces a double-digit DPU increase, ask where the extra money came from.
Can that same source support another increase next year?

title: Get Smart: “I Should Have Sold”
article:
Around eight weeks.
That’s all it took to send the Singapore market into a 10% decline.
But if you plan to invest well, give yourself eight years or longer.
We’ll go one better.
If you measure yourself over eight weeks, you are setting yourself up for one of two things: disappointment or, worse, delusion.
When the stock market runs ahead of itself
Coming into the earnings season, Singapore banks were already priced at high valuations, a point I raised during my CNA
segment
last month.
That meant they had a lot to live up to.
And when the banks don’t deliver what the market expects, shares get sold off — starting with
United Overseas Bank
(SGX: U11), or UOB, last Wednesday (4 November 2026).
Here’s the twist.
UOB’s third-quarter net profit almost tripled year on year to S$1.25 billion, boosted by a favourable comparison with the same quarter a year ago.
Yet the result still fell short of the roughly S$1.37 billion that analysts had expected.
In response, shares have fallen by nearly 9% to under S$37 as of last Friday.
Make no mistake.
Profits almost tripled, and the shares still fell.
That’s what happens when the stock market runs ahead of the business.
Thank you, Captain Obvious
I can hear the critics up in arms.
If you knew bank stocks were going to fall, why didn’t you sell?
This is the false idea that a “good investor” is able to sniff out a price fall before it happens.
It looks obvious.
But only in hindsight.
In reality, bank shares have traded above their historical price-to-book (P/B) ratios — the price you pay for every dollar of a bank’s net assets — since the second half of 2024.
Take UOB.
On 26 August 2024, its shares were at just under S$31, or 1.2 times book value — already above its historical average.
If you sold back then, planning to buy the shares back later at a lower price, you’d have been mistaken.
Even after last week’s slide, UOB shares are still nearly 20% higher.
And that’s before counting the dividends you’d have given up.
Believing we could have called the fall is the delusion I mentioned at the start.
As author Thomas Phelps once said:
“Most deception is bad but self-deception is worse because it is done to such a nice guy!”
Get Smart: Don’t grade yourself on hindsight
Here’s the thing about eight weeks.
Measure yourself during a slide, and you’ll be disappointed.
Measure yourself after it, and you’ll convince yourself you saw it coming.
Neither tells you whether you’re a good investor.
Eight weeks tells you the market’s mood.
Eight years tells you the business.
So, as the banks report their results, skip the question “Should I have sold?”
Ask instead: “Is the business still growing its profits and dividends?”
That’s what will be focused on at the Smart Dividend Portfolio this week.
A market decline is not an obituary.
Instead, it is a chance to pick up shares that have been unfairly sold off.

title: 3 SGX Stocks Outpacing the STI YTD
article:
The
SPDR STI ETF
(SGX: ES3), which tracks Singapore’s
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI), had a bumpy October.
Step back, though, and the fund still delivered a total return of 18.7% for the year to date (YTD).
In fact, a few smaller names did much better.
Micro-Mechanics (Holdings) Ltd
(SGX: 5DD) returned 58.1% over the same period, including dividends, while
Nanofilm Technologies International Limited
(SGX: MZH) and
Civmec Limited (SGX: P9D)
returned 39% and 36%, respectively.
So what sets these three apart?
Share prices move for many reasons, but their latest results hint at one possible answer.
Profits grew faster than sales, and each company had work lined up.
Investors may be paying up for that combination.
What’s behind Micro-Mechanics’ record quarter?
Micro-Mechanics
makes precision tools and parts for semiconductor manufacturing.
For the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (1QFY2027), ended 30 September 2026, revenue rose 45% year on year (YoY) to a record S$24.2 million.
Its Consumable Tools division, which brought in 75.8% of that revenue, helps chipmakers cut defects and improve yields.
Net profit grew even faster, up 102.8% to S$6.4 million, also a quarterly record.
How did profit outrun revenue?
Two words: wider margins.
Gross margin hit a 20-quarter high of 55%, up from 51.5%, while overheads fell to 20.7% of revenue from 25.1%.
Build-to-Print sales rose 97.5% as bookings picked up and material shortages eased.
Management sees
strong demand tied to AI
, computing and memory chips.
Its five-year plan aims to double revenue from FY2026 levels to at least S$150 million.
The cash flow statement, however, tells a quieter story.
Free cash flow slipped 10.6% YoY to S$3.7 million as trade receivables grew and capital expenditure rose to S$0.9 million from S$0.3 million.
The company plans to spend S$12 million this year on expanding capacity.
It holds S$33.3 million in cash and no bank borrowings.
Micro-Mechanics declared no dividend this quarter, as it pays only in the second and fourth quarters.
Management is watching the Middle East conflict’s effect on costs and supply chains.
How did Nanofilm grow profit 165.6% on 6.1% revenue growth?
Nanofilm produces advanced material coatings and nanofabricated products.
It reports half-yearly, so its figures cover January to June 2026, earlier than the other two.
In the first half of 2026 (1H2026), revenue rose 6.1% YoY to S$113.7 million.
Profit attributable to equity holders grew 165.6% to S$4.3 million.
Here’s the thing: margins made the difference.
Gross margin widened to 38.6% from 32.6%, which Nanofilm credits to productivity gains, automation and cost discipline.
Those savings more than offset a 56.6% rise in R&D and engineering expenses.
Free cash flow turned positive at S$19.5 million, against negative S$10.3 million a year ago, as receivables collection got better.
Nanofilm also raised its interim dividend to S$0.006 per share, from S$0.003.
As at 30 June 2026, it held S$88.7 million in cash against S$88.8 million in bank loans.
Management expects the Industrial Equipment Business Unit (IEBU) order backlog to support stronger deliveries in 2026’s second half, with visibility into 2027.
On the flip side, the profit growth comes off a small base.
IEBU and Sydrogen (its hydrogen-energy business) revenue fell 28.7% and 43.6% YoY, respectively, on lower equipment sales and project delays.
Tighter memory chip supply and rising component prices may keep pressure on costs.
Can Civmec’s order book sustain the momentum?
Headquartered in Henderson, Western Australia,
Civmec
provides heavy engineering, construction, maintenance and naval shipbuilding services.
For 1QFY2027, ended 30 September 2026, revenue rose 70.2% YoY to a record A$324 million.
Net profit after tax grew 75.2% to A$18.4 million, and net profit margin improved to 5.7% from 5.5%.
Its construction division drove the growth as major projects ramped up, including BHP’s Port Debottlenecking Project 2 and Iluka Resources’ Eneabba Rare Earths Refinery.
As at 29 October 2026, Civmec’s order book stood at around A$1.4 billion, up from A$1.15 billion a year ago.
On 5 October 2026, it announced more than A$220 million in new contract awards and extensions for delivery across FY2027 and FY2028.
It pays dividends half-yearly.
Its FY2026 dividends totalled A$0.060, including a final A$0.035 paid on 23 October 2026.
There are gaps, though.
The quarterly update had no cash flow statement or balance sheet, so investors cannot see free cash flow or debt.
A 5.7% net margin also leaves little room for cost overruns, and management gave no guidance for FY2027.
Get Smart: Is the cash keeping up with the profits?
When profits grow faster than sales, a business keeps more of each dollar it earns.
Dividend investors should ask one more question: is the cash following?
Micro-Mechanics doubled its profit, yet free cash flow fell.
Nanofilm is the opposite, with free cash flow well above profit.
So when a stock beats the index, don’t stop at the profit line.
Compare free cash flow with net profit over several periods.
Then ask whether the margin gains came from lasting changes or from conditions that may fade.
